parts.name: Thermal camera: FLIR Lepton 3.5 on a PureThermal 3 board
parts.size: Lepton 11.8 × 12.7 × 7.2 mm on a 32 × 32 mm board, in a 40 × 30 × 22 mm printed case
parts.job: Measures the temperature of the shrub canopy, looking straight down.
parts.why: When chaparral shrubs run short of water they close their leaf pores and the leaves warm up compared with the air; leaf-minus-air temperature is a standard plant water-stress signal, and the one sensor here that works in the pre-dawn flight too. 160 × 120 pixels, radiometric. At 60 m one pixel covers about 0.4 m; with lens blur and motion, only shrubs of about 2 m or more give pure canopy pixels, smaller ones mix with soil. Its accuracy (about ±5 °C) is not enough alone, so warm and cool targets of known temperature sit in every flight, and the camera is kept in an insulated case and warmed up in a hover before the survey.
parts.without: No measure of plant stress: leaf temperature against air temperature is the only stress signal the drone has. The papers below are on irrigated crops and orchards, not chaparral; how well it works over shrubs is part of what the first flights test.

refs.cite: Jackson et al., Water Resources Research 17:1133 (1981)
refs.says: canopy temperature as a water stress indicator (the crop water stress index)

refs.cite: Berni et al., IEEE Trans. Geoscience and Remote Sensing 47:722 (2009)
refs.says: a small drone with an inexpensive thermal camera (40 cm pixels) mapped water stress from canopy temperature, checked on the ground

refs.cite: Gonzalez-Dugo et al., Precision Agriculture 14:660 (2013)
refs.says: drone thermal images used to map the water status of five tree species in one orchard

refs.cite: Aragon et al., Sensors 20:3316 (2020)
refs.says: calibrating a FLIR A655sc pixel by pixel against a lab black body cut its error from about 6 °C to under 1 °C; not tested on a Lepton

parts.instead: FLIR Boson 320 or a Workswell WIRIS (thousands of dollars, asked by email): sharper images, but the same need for ground targets to be accurate.
parts.source: Jackson et al. 1981 (crop water stress index); FLIR Lepton 3.5 datasheet; BEST_PRICES 10 Nov

With a 6 mm lens at 60 m one pixel is 3.5 cm and a photo covers 50 × 38 m; flown with the short side along the track, 2 photos a second give 75 % overlap at 19 m/s, enough to build the canopy's 3D shape (photogrammetry). A global shutter takes the whole frame at once, so the picture does not skew at speed; 1 ms exposure smears 1.9 cm, under one pixel. Needs daylight, so it is not used in the pre-dawn flight.
parts.without: We could not find the same shrub at dawn and at midday, or tell leaf from soil. At midday bare soil is far hotter than leaves, so a thermal pixel that mixes in soil looks like a stressed shrub.

refs.cite: Dandois and Ellis, Remote Sensing of Environment 136:259 (2013)
refs.says: 3D canopy structure from overlapping photos taken with an ordinary camera on a hobby drone below 130 m

parts.instead: Livox Mid-360 lidar (265 g, 6.5 W): it looks sideways and up, and reaches only 40 m, so it cannot map the ground from 60 m. MAPIR Survey3W ($400) adds a near-infrared band.
parts.source: Raspberry Pi camera specs; Livox Mid-360 specs (read 18 Nov); our ground-resolution arithmetic

parts.name: 1610 nm spot sensor (built by us): two InGaAs photodiodes behind 1610 nm filters
parts.size: 50 × 40 × 45 mm printed head with a 20° view tube
parts.job: Measures how much 1610 nm short-wave infrared light the shrubs reflect, one reading per spot, plus the sunlight coming down.
parts.why: Water in leaves absorbs strongly near 1600 nm, so reflectance in this band drops as leaves hold less water; it is the standard leaf-water band. A camera for this band costs $5,650 or more (LUCID Triton SWIR) or rents for $2,250 a week, so for the first flights we build a two-channel sensor: one diode looks down through a 20° tube (a 21 m spot at 60 m), one looks up through a diffuser to read the sunlight. Parts $385 plus about $25 of small parts. It needs sunlight, so it works from the morning flight on, not before dawn. Readings taken while the drone banks in a turn are dropped, using the bank angle from the flight controller, because the upward diode then sees the sky at an angle. Each spot mixes shrub, soil and shadow, which is why the near-infrared channel below is worth adding.
parts.without: We would see stress (leaf pores closing) but have no reading tied to how much water the leaves hold. The band responds to water per leaf area; live fuel moisture, which fire planners use, is water per dry mass, so the two are related, not the same. Open risk: the change between dawn and midday may be too small for this band to see; the first flights test that.

refs.cite: Hunt and Rock, Remote Sensing of Environment 30:43 (1989)
refs.says: changes in leaf water content detected with near- and middle-infrared reflectance

refs.cite: Ceccato et al., Remote Sensing of Environment 77:22 (2001)
refs.says: detecting leaf water content from reflectance in the optical bands

refs.cite: Yebra et al., Remote Sensing of Environment 136:455 (2013)
refs.says: review of remote sensing of live fuel moisture for fire danger

parts.instead: A SWIR camera through the companies we emailed (LUCID, Tech Imaging rental, SILIOS, Spectral Devices): images instead of spots, $2,250 a week to $30,000.
parts.source: Hunt and Rock 1989, Ceccato et al. 2001 (leaf water in the short-wave infrared); SPOT_SENSOR_CIRCUIT doc; prices BEST_PRICES 10 Nov

parts.name: Air temperature and humidity: Sensirion SHT45
parts.size: 25 × 18 mm board in a small printed sun shield
parts.job: Measures the air temperature and humidity at the drone, every flight.
parts.why: Leaf temperature only means stress when compared with the air around it and how dry that air is (vapour pressure deficit). The weather meter on the ground is the main reference at canopy height; this sensor adds the air at flight height, which at dawn can differ by several degrees because of the morning temperature inversion. ±0.1 °C and ±1 % humidity; checked against the ground meter in the shade before each flight, and mounted in a small shield away from the electronics.
parts.without: The weather meter on the ground still gives the air near the canopy, so stress can still be read. What is lost is the air at flight height, which at dawn can be several degrees different because of the morning temperature inversion.

refs.cite: Idso et al., Agricultural Meteorology 24:45 (1981)
refs.says: leaf-minus-air temperature has to be normalised for the weather, mainly how dry the air is, before it means stress

parts.instead: Ground weather meter only: it is the main reference anyway, but misses the air the drone flies through.
parts.source: Adafruit SHT45 page (read 18 Nov); Idso et al. 1981

parts.name: Near-infrared reference channel (850 nm) for the spot sensor
parts.size: two silicon photodiodes and filters in the spot sensor head
buy: Edmund Optics 850 nm / 40 nm bandpass, 12.5 mm mounted (×2)
parts.job: Adds a near-infrared band next to the 1610 nm band, down and up, in the same head.
parts.why: Leaves reflect strongly at 850 nm and water barely absorbs there, so the ratio of the 1610 nm and 850 nm readings cancels most of the effect of lighting and shadow. Soil still mixes in; the colour camera's plant and soil split corrects for that. Pairing a water band with a near-infrared band is the usual leaf-water index. Two filters (most of the $214) and two silicon photodiodes on the same converter.
parts.without: The 1610 nm reading would also change with lighting, shadow and how much of the 21 m spot is soil, not only with leaf water.

refs.cite: Hunt and Rock, Remote Sensing of Environment 30:43 (1989)
refs.says: changes in leaf water content detected with near- and middle-infrared reflectance

refs.cite: Gao, Remote Sensing of Environment 58:257 (1996)
refs.says: a water index from two near-infrared bands (860 and 1240 nm), one absorbed by water and one not

parts.instead: 1240 nm band (InGaAs, $123 filter): a second water band, but more expensive.
parts.source: Hunt and Rock 1989; Ceccato et al. 2001; Edmund Optics listing

mounts.name: Avionics cassette (removable tray in the nose)
mounts.fastening: 2 tongues slide down vertical grooves in 2 rail blocks (F1, F2); 2 captive M3 thumb screws through the end-wall tabs into heat-set inserts in the rail blocks. Cube carrier hard-mounted on 4 M3 nylon standoffs (the Cube isolates its IMUs inside); radios and Remote ID on hook-and-loop through deck slots; PM07 on 4 M3 standoffs on the aft wall.
remove_steps: Lift the avionics hatch off (magnets).
Unplug the battery XT90 in the battery bay (or keep the battery out).

Unplug at the cassette: 5 ESC feeds (XT60) and 2 XT30 (servo regulator, payload) from the PM07 leads; servo/ESC signal leads from the carrier servo rail (9 x 3-pin, labelled M1-M5, A1-A4); GPS (GPS1), airspeed (I2C), payload MAVLink (TELEM2).
Undo the 2 thumb screws (they stay in the tabs).
Lift the cassette straight up by its two end-wall handles (110 mm).
mounts.time_note: estimate [A]: ~20 plugs at ~8 s + screws + hatch; not timed on hardware. USB and microSD of the Cube are reachable with the hatch off, without removing anything.

connectors.faces: hatch side (mated pair lies on top of the pack front in the battery bay)
hatch side (pigtails out of the aft cable window)

connectors.connector: servo rail 0.1 in headers (MAIN 1-5 ESCs, AUX 1-4 servos)
connectors.faces: hatch side (+y end of the carrier, turned 90 deg) [A: MEASURE on the ADS-B carrier]

mounts.wiring_route: Power: battery XT90 in the battery bay -> PM07 lead over the F2 ring (frames are open rings) -> PM07 on the cassette aft wall; 5 ESC feeds + 2 XT30 leave by the aft cable windows with a 100 mm slack loop each, then run aft along the left fuselage wall beside the battery (y 68..83 gap) to the wing root. Signals: carrier servo rail leads run aft along the right wall; GPS lead up into the wing root; airspeed I2C forward through F1. Labels: every lead gets a printed label in heat shrink at both ends (M1..M5, A1..A4, GPS, I2C, TEL2, BAT, ESC1..5, SREG, PAY).

mounts.name: Belly sensor plate (removable, with the Pi deck)
mounts.fastening: 4 captive M3 thumb screws up into heat-set inserts in bosses on frames F3 and F4; sensors on corner posts with 1 zip tie each; Pi 5 on 4 M2.5 nylon standoffs on the deck; deck on 4 legs, M3 screws from below into inserts.
remove_steps: Turn the drone over (or reach under it on its stand).
Undo the 4 thumb screws (they stay in the plate).
Lower the plate ~60 mm on its pigtails.
Unplug the 2 plugs: XT30 power and JST-GH 6-pin MAVLink.
Take the whole sensor set to the bench.

connectors.connector: JST-GH 6-pin (UART on the Pi GPIO via adapter)

mounts.wiring_route: Both airframe leads come from the cassette along the fuselage floor under the battery tray (z -102..-165 is empty now) to x ~40, slack loop at the plate. All sensor cables (USB to the PureThermal, CSI ribbon, I2C to the spot sensor and SHT45) stay on the plate.

mounts.name: Tail-cone access panel (pusher ESC + servo regulator ride on it)
mounts.fastening: 4 M3 x 8 button-head screws into heat-set inserts in 4 small blocks bonded on the end ledges; the existing ESC tray and regulator mount are bonded to the panel instead of the shell floor; ESC and regulator on 2 cable ties each

mounts.wiring_route: Feeds come aft along the left fuselage wall from the cassette over the battery bay floor and through F4; 150 mm slack each at the panel so it drops without unplugging.
